Multiplayer

Choose a multiplayer model

2 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Choose the unit of stateChoose who decidesKeep presentation separateTest one contested interaction

Three decisions shape a multiplayer game: where gameplay state lives, whose result settles a conflict, and which moment each screen displays. Choose them before adding a transport. A host/client role alone does not define all three.

Choose the unit of state#

Model Where you write gameplay How correction is organized Start here
Kit Script structs, tagged entity fields, generated commands, and optional fixed ticks Target-local command prediction and the simulation lane's historical state Build a Kit game
Replay A typed World stepped from inputs, with Godot views outside the simulation Complete-frame restoration and replay for the authored simulation group Build a Replay game

Kit supports both cooperative owner movement and server-authoritative prediction. Replay supports server authority, cooperative owner streams, and deterministic peer rollback. Choose by the game's state dependencies and trust model rather than treating the frameworks as a co-op/competitive switch.

Choose who decides#

Invited co-op. Players can author their own motion while the host validates shared interactions. Kit's owner fields are a small starting point. Replay's owner streams can record accepted Godot body observations when the game uses live engine physics.

Listen-server action. The hosting player runs the authority. Clients submit intent, predict locally, and accept corrections. This is convenient for player-hosted sessions; the host still controls the authoritative process.

Dedicated authority. A process on trusted infrastructure judges the game. Validate game-specific input, choose admission and transport policy, and plan deployment and recovery. In Kit, the dedicated profile also requires constrained or validated simulation inputs. In Replay, Session exposes an avatarless Server role, with Room policies available for trusted infrastructure recovery.

Deterministic peers. Admitted players exchange inputs and reproduce the same steps. Replay's P2P runner requires fixed roster identities and a simulation that reproduces math, RNG, allocation, and input order across its target platforms. Use the Duel example for that contract.

Keep presentation separate#

Local prediction responds to current input. Remote interpolation usually presents a buffered past. Effects need to follow the frame being displayed; applying a remote pickup effect as soon as a packet arrives can make the item vanish before the visible player reaches it.

Godot rigid-body solving needs an explicit policy. Saving node poses does not restore contact solving. Use a replayable query-based model or cooperative body observations according to the game you are building.

Test one contested interaction#

Give two players one item. Let both predict taking it, delay the connection, and make one request lose. Check the inventories, entity lifetime, and the record of presented effects. This exposes the state and presentation boundaries before a large game makes the failure difficult to isolate.

Continue with Kit profiles, Replay's runner guide, and timeline choices. The illustrated field guide follows this pickup through both frameworks with diagrams and a correction lab.
